title: PE Exam Practice Problem #4: Water Resources | Peak Flow
problem_statement: A given Community has a current population of 30,000 residents the town has recently started to smell funny and their sports teams are all doing poorly as such it has been predicted that their population will decrease by about 25% over the next 10 years as people move away in disgust however this smelly unathletic town is also concerned about climate change and the larger storms that are expected to impact it in 10 years the wastewater treatment plant is planning to change their Peak flow capacity from 2.5 times the daily flow to three times the daily flow what is the new Peak flow expected to be in 10 years in MGD so this is a long problem to read out but it's actually a very short one to solve the first thing to note about this problem is that it doesn't require anything from the reference manual it gives you everything you need to solve it right within the problem so let's get to it.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Is to find the future expected water use in 10 years we
solution_steps.explanation: Step one is to find the future expected water use in 10 years we're just going to sum the commercial and domestic flows that are expected 10 years later so from our table over here we can see that 10 years later the expected commercial use in gallons per cap per day is 8 and the domestic is 45 so 8 + 45 simply equals 53 gallons per capita per day.

solution_steps.title: Step 2: We're going to find the new expected population in 10 y

pollutants from its effluent flows initial concentration of 75 mg per liter the river has an existing flow rate of 225 CFS (ft³/s) and an existing pollution concentration of 1 mg per liter the pollution limits in this River are not to exceed a concentration of 3 Mig per liter what is the max flow rate that the factory can discharge in million gallons per day so as not to exceed the river's pollution limit so this problem is a pretty classic example of a mass balance problem that you would find in an undergraduate environmental engineering class I don't even think there is an equation for it in the reference manual but the closest I found is on page 460 if you want to see an example of a mass balance equation used for a slightly different application the version of the mass balance equation that we want to use can instead be written as follows q1 c1+ Q2 C2 equal Q3 C3 and in this case Q3 is going to be a combination of q1 plus Q2 so let's get into the problem the question is problem_statement: A water quality engineer is determining the max concentration of a compound that can be released into a water supply the following data are provided the no observed adverse effect level Noel for this compound was found to be 14.28 mg per kilogram day it was assumed that the average person weighed 70 kg and would consume 2 L of water per day an uncertainty fact factor of 10 was applied for interspecies differences between the test animals and humans and another uncertainty factor of 10 is applied to account for variation in human sensitivity what should the maximum contaminant level goal or mclg be for this compound in drinking water in milligrams per liter so in this problem the first thing we need to do is to find the equations we need if we search Noel in the reference manual this will bring us to section 6.7.8 titled risk calculation the reference manual provides two equations that are required for this problem the first is the reference dose which equals the Noel divided by the uncertainty Factor the second is the DW or drinking water equivalent level which is the reference dose times body weight divided by drinking water consumption or dwc to shorten that next let's write out our know and what we are looking for so the problem gives us the Noel already and that is going to be 14.28 millgram per kilogram day the body weight used in the study was understand how to manipulate the equation for reference dose to go into the equation for dwel and finally you need to recognize that both uncertainty factors need to be used to account for the total uncertainty used in coming up with this standard and that's it.

problem_statement: A water quality engineer is determining the max concentration of a compound that can be released into a water supply the following data are provided the no observed adverse effect level Noel for this compound was found to be 14.28 mg per kilog day it was assumed that the average person weighed 70 kg and would consume 2 L of water per day an uncertainty fact factor of 10 was applied for inters species differences between the test animals and humans and another uncertainty factor of 10 is applied to account for variation in human sensitivity what should the maximum contaminant level goal or mclg be for this compound in drinking water in milligrams per liter so in this problem the first thing we need to do is to find the equations we need if we search Noel in the reference manual this will bring us to section 6.7.8 titled risk calculation the reference manual provides two equations that are required for this problem the first is the reference dose which equals the Noel divided by the uncertainty Factor the second is the dwe or drinking water equivalent level which is the reference dose times body weight divided by drinking water consumption or dwc to shorten that next let's write out our know and what we are looking for so the problem gives us the Noel already and that is going to be 14.28 millgram per kilogram day the body weight used in the study was given as 70 kg and the drinking water consumption we're going to shorten to dwc is given as 2 L per day there are two uncertainty factors given we can write out uf1 = 10 and uf2 = 10 and finally we're being asked to find the maximum contaminant level goal or mclg so what does it take to solve this problem now that we have everything we need laid out first we need to realize that the mclg we are asked to solve for is actually the term dwel in one of our equations next we need to recognize that while we aren't given the reference dose we are given the terms that comprise this variable so let's rewrite our equation to include those terms instead now all we have to do is plug in our given and solve the problem so mclg is going to be 14.28 millgram per kilogram Day times 70 kg over our first uncertainty factor of 10 times our second uncertainty factor of 10 times our drinking water consumption of 2 L per day and if we solve this out first of all we can cancel some units to determine that we're in the right units still and we can see here that the end result is milligrams per liter and our answer is just about five which we can see is one of our answers over here so this problem is actually very easy to solve if you know a few things one you need to know where your equations come from in the manual two you need to recognize that the mclg equals the dwel and three you need to understand how to manipulate the equation for reference dose to go into the equation for dwe and finally you need to recognize that both uncertainty factors need to be used to account for the total uncertainty used in coming up with this standard and that's it.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #53: Transportation | Traffic Counts - Average Daily Volume
problem_statement: Continuous daily traffic counts are recorded on Street 1 and are given in the following table. A similar street on the other side of town also exists Street 2, where continuous traffic counts were taken on a Thursday. If the traffic is assumed to be proportional between these streets each day of the week, estimate the average daily traffic volume over the week for Street 2. So this problem is pretty straightforward. We have a week's worth of traffic counts for Street 1 and we are being asked to find the average daily traffic volume for Street 2. Section 5.1.3.1 of the reference manual covers average daily traffic values but doesn't give us a specific equation to use. In this case, we need to recognize that the average for the week is going to be a regular average, summing the daily volumes in Street 1 and dividing by the number of days in a week. Since the problem notes that the traffic is assumed to be proportional between these streets on each day of the week, all we need to do is find the ratio of Street 2 to Street 1 on Thursday. The day when measurements were taken on both streets and then adjust Street 1's average daily volume accordingly. So let's get to it. The first thing we're going to do is get the ratio between Street 2 and Street 1 on Thursday. So that's going to be 8756 over 10842, which is going to give us about 0.8. Next, we can find the average daily traffic volume for Street 1. And that's going to be a sum of the following days of the week divided by the number of days in the week. So we're going to do 76433 plus 11, 11, 10 plus 8176 plus 9632 plus 10, 842 plus 12, 3, 2, 0, plus 9405 plus 8176 plus 9. Over 7 and that's going to give us 69128 over 7, which is going to give us 9875. So that's the ADT for Street 1. Assuming proportionality between the two streets like the problem mentions, all we need to do now is multiply the ratio for Thursday that we came up with by Street 1's ADT. And that will give us 7975, which is the ADT for Street 2. And that's all it takes to solve this problem.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #54: Materials | Geotechnical - Vertical Stress
problem_statement: A big fancy house is built as shown and in parts 300 pounds per square foot of vertical stress onto the ground beneath it. Find the effective vertical stress in pounds per square foot at the given point in the soil profile depicted. So in the given figure, we can see our big fancy house imparting 300 PSF to the soil beneath that we can see point A located in the clay and we can see all of the respective depths relative to each other item. We also have the groundwater level called out and the respective densities of the sand and the clay. So all we need to do is find the effective vertical stress at point A. So the first thing we can do is note that the stress increases both with the depth and the density or unit weight of whatever soil is above that depth. So the first thing we can do is consider the stress just from the house and this number is given to us directly as 300 PSF. Keep in mind that those are the units we are looking for anyway. Next we need to find the effective stress in just the dry sand. So the section of sand to the depth of the groundwater level will be dry and that's going to be 8 feet. So the effective vertical stress for this layer is going to be the unit weight of the dry sand times the depth of the dry sand. And this is going to give us 880 pounds per square foot. Next we can calculate the effective vertical stress in the saturated sand. So if the total depth of the sand is 10 feet and the total dry depth is 8 feet then the total saturated sand is going to be 2 feet. So when calculating the saturated effective vertical stress it's important to remember that any load carried by the saturated soil is carried by both the grains of soil and also the poor pressure of the water. So in this case we are actually going to be subtracting out the density of water from the density of our saturated sand. So first we are going to subtract 110 pounds per cubic foot by 62.4 pounds per cubic foot which is the unit weight of water. And you can look that up in the reference manual if you don't have that memorized. And we are going to multiply it by the saturated depth of 2 feet. And this is going to give us about 95.2 pounds per foot squared. And finally we can solve for the effective vertical stress in the clay up to the given point here. So if the total depth of clay is 10 feet and we know the point is 5 feet above the bottom of the clay layer then the depth of clay remaining will be 5 feet. So just as we did before with the saturated sand we can subtract 62.4 from the unit weight of the clay. And then multiply by the depth to which we are going. And this will give us 188 pounds per square foot. So if we sum up each of the vertical stresses that we calculated from 1 to 4 we are going to see that our total effect of vertical stress is about 1463 pounds per square foot which we can see is our second answer. A few things to point out for this problem would be to first remember to account for the ground water at the depth that it exists and not to try to solve the problem for a deeper point in the layer than the point being asked for. Finally remember to account for the stress in the house that was given directly. The height of the house does not matter but the height of the soil layers does because we were only given density instead of effective stress. But that is all it takes to solve this problem.

Now we can move on to using general knowledge, context clues, and process of elimination. problem_statement: A building exists on a plot next to which an 8-foot-deep excavation is being made. According to the OSHA technical manual regarding excavations, the soil in this area has been classified as Type C. It is desired to leave some amount of horizontal perimeter strip next to the building. What is the maximum permissible width of this perimeter strip in feet? So, all this problem really requires is finding the slope of the slope requirements for Type C soil, and then solving for some basic geometry. So, we have our excavation depth here, the total distance away from the building in question here, and we need to know how much distance might be available for a strip perimeter strip, depending on the value of the slope or the steepness of the grid. So, the first thing we can do is we can search either OSHA or Type C into our reference manual, and that only is to section 3.10.3 slope configurations in layered soils. The problem doesn't mention anything about multiple layers of soil, so we can assume that there is only one layer. So, as we can see in our table, our excavation for Type C soil is less than 20 feet deep, and the slope requirements are 1.5 horizontal to one vertical. So, we want to know how much room there is for a perimeter strip. So, we need to know the horizontal length of the slope. Solving this equation will give that to us. So, we know that 1.5 over 1, which is going to be x over y, equals x, which we don't know yet over on this side, and y is going to be 8 feet. So, solving for this, x equals 12 feet. So, finally, all we have to do, we can find the space available for a perimeter strip by subtracting the horizontal length of the excavation from the total horizontal distance from the bottom of the excavation to the building. So, we now know that there is going to be 12 feet of space required, the horizontal length required for a slope of Type C soil, meaning that if we have 15 feet and we need 12 feet, then 3 feet of horizontal distance will be left over here for a perimeter strip. And that's all it takes to solve this problem. Simply knowing where to find your slope for Type C soil, and then how to apply it with some basic math. And that's it.

topic: Soil Selection Using USCS Method - Concept
problem_statement: A contractor is attempting to mitigate moisture intrusion from the soil into the proposed building's subsurface wall. It is also desired to mitigate additional stresses on the building. The contractor has access to various materials at a local baro pit, with which they can construct a barrier between the soil and the wall. According to the Unified Soil Classification System, which of the following options below is most suitable for their goals? So this is another concept problem. The goal is to use the USCIS soil classification chart to decide which of our options will be best in terms of two goals, mitigating both moisture intrusion and stresses upon the structure. So go to that table and let's go through our options. First, the chart tells us that SW is a well graded sand. This is usually used in drainage, so would serve the opposite purpose of our goal of mitigating moisture intrusion. This sand would allow moisture to easily pass through it, which is a good thing if our stated goal was to drain moisture rather than prevent its intrusion. The above case is an example of which type of steel failure, fatigue, expansion, deformation, or deflection. This is an example of a conceptual problem that we would not be able to use the reference manual to help us with. Instead, it is a case where we would need to understand what is happening in the case provided and recognize the type of failure that occurred. In this case, the problem states that the dump truck is routinely loaded to 12,000 pounds, which is less than its maximum carrying capacity of 13,000 pounds. The fact that this is the same capacity at which the thrust rod failed can be understood to be an example of fatigue. Fatigue type failures are due to a reduction in strength due to cyclical loading. The problem does not provide any more detail as to what exactly happened to the thrust rod, so it would be a stretch to guess that any of the other type of failures listed here were the cause. I think it is important to study questions like this simply to be aware of the fact that some things are not going to be in the reference manual. This is the type of information that would have been covered in many introductory materials classes and is probably why questions like these are fair game on the civil PE. dividing the concentration that we are given by the equivalent weight of the ion we have the concentrations so now we just need to find the equivalent weight this is available in the manual in A new screw pump is being added which will handle an additional 10 million gallons per day during wet weather and be used to control the depth of water in the wet well. The wet well is 20 ft deep. The average daily flow at the treatment plant is 10 MGD and the required chlorine demand is 50 lb per hour. This is achieved by two chlorinator units each with a max dosing rate of 10 mg per liter as Cl2 currently dosing a combined concentration of 7 mg per liter into this flow. If a mass of,200 lb of chlorine is used per day during disinfection, find the daily peaking factor that was used in the current operation of this treatment plant. So this problem has a very long problem statement. However, all it is asking us to find is the peaking factor that accompanies a certain concentration of chlorine. If you go to section 6.7.1 mass conservation and continuity there is a section called the concentration to mass per day conversion. Here it gives us the exact equation that we need to solve this problem. It's given as mass m in units of pounds per day equals a concentration C in units of mg per liter times Q which is our flow in units of MGD. times our conversion of 8.34. And the units for this is going to be pounds per million gallons over mg per liter. So once we know what equation to use, we can see that this question is actually extremely simple to solve and that only a small subset of the information given in the problem is required. We don't need anything about the screw pump, the wet well or the max dosing rates of the two chlorinator units. We don't even necessarily need the information about the chlorine demand in pounds per hour since we are given the chlorine demand in pounds per day. All.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #85: Water Resources/Environmental | Wastewater BOD5 Removal Efficiency
problem_statement: A wastewater treatment plant uses an activated sludge process following a primary clarifier. The plant receives an average daily flow of 3 MGD with an influent BOD5 concentration of 250 mg per liter and an influent suspended solids concentration of 300 mg per liter. The treatment process consists of a primary clarifier that removes 35% of the incoming BOD5 and 60% of the suspended solids. An aerration tank that follows the primary clarifier and removes additional BOD5 and suspended solids. The combined treatment processes of the primary clarifier and aeration tank together remove 5,645 lbs per day of BOD5 and 7,55 lbs per day of suspended solids. What is most nearly the BOD5 removal efficiency within the aerration tank? So the first thing we can see in this problem is recognize that we need to find the BOD5 removal efficiency of the aation tank. This means that all of the information provided about the suspended solids can be ignored. Let's find the answer to what we're looking for in four steps. So.

solution_steps.title: Step 1: Step 1 Calculation
solution_steps.explanation: For step one, our goal is to find the total BOD5 entering the plant. To solve for this, we simply need to multiply the average daily flow of 3 MGD times a conversion factor of 8.34 pounds per million gallon over mg per liter. and then multiply this times the influent BOD5 concentration of 250 mg per  liter. And we can see that the total BOD5 entering the plant is 6,255 pounds per day.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #95: Water Resources/Environmental | Ion Exchange/Softening/Target Hardness
problem_statement: A municipal utility treats groundwater to reduce hardness using an ion exchange softener. The untreated water characteristics were recorded during testing and are in the provided table. The softener reduces hardness effectively, but still allows a leakage hardness of 10 mg per liter as CA3 in the treated stream. To maintain corrosion control while also preserving taste, the utility blends some untreated groundwater with the softened water to produce a finished water hardness of 90 mg per liter at CA3. What percentage of untreated groundwater should be bypassed and blended with the softened water to achieve the desired finished water quality? The possible percentages are 24%, 27%, 30%, and 33%. So in this problem, the ultimate goal is to figure out what percentage of the groundwater can be bypassed during the ion exchange softener. That means that the first thing we have to do is figure out which of the parameters contribute to hardness in the problem. Hardness in water is caused mainly by two ions, calcium and magnesium. These are naturally present in ground water and surface water and they're the reason for that chalky buildup on faucets or the need for extra soap. So in this problem, we are going to be pulling out the values for calcium and magnesium. For step two of the problem, we are going to convert calcium and magnesium from milligs per liter into mill equivalents per liter. This standardizes the concentrations based on each ion's charge and molecular weight. So to find the miller equivalents per liter, we have the concentration, but we need to go into the reference manual and find the equivalent weight for each parameter. In version 1.6 of the environmental reference manual, page 22 contains a table called common radicals in water. This is one place in the manual from which you can obtain these numbers. So the equivalent weight of calcium is going to be 20 and the equivalent weight of magnesium is going to be about 12.2. So to convert calcium we will divide our concentration of 72 mg per liter by the equivalent weight of 20 to get 3.6 mill equivalents per liter. Then we can divide the concentration for magnesium of 18 mg per liter by its equivalent weight of 12.2 and get just about 1.5 mill equivalents per liter. The total hardness in this problem will be the sum of these two values totaling 5.1 mil equivalents per liter. Now that we are halfway through our conversion in step three, we can convert from mill equivalents per liter to mg per liter as Ca3.  In many water softening problems, hardness is reported as milligrams per liter as calcium carbonate or CO3 because it provides a consistent basis for comparison among many parameters. To do this, we can multiply the total miller equivalent per liter by Ca3's equivalent weight of 50, also found in the reference manual. 5.1 mill equivalents per liter time 50 gives us just about 255 mg per liter as Ca3. That's going to be the raw water hardness. Finally, we can apply the bypass fraction formula here to determine the percentage of water that needs to be bypassed in order to achieve the given finished water hardness.  The equation for bypass hardness is going to be the finished hardness minus the leakage hardness over the raw hardness minus the leakage hardness.  The problem statement itself gives us the finished hardness of 90 mg per liter as Ca3 and the leakage hardness of 10 mg per liter as Ca3. On the bottom of the equation, we've calculated the raw hardness to be 253 mg per liter SCA3. And again, our leakage is going to be 10 mg per liter SCA3. We can ignore these units since they are all the same. And finally, we can see that our answer is 33%. Or the fourth answer below. So the big points to this problem are understanding which parameters you need when thinking about hardness, converting those to mill equivalents per liter and summing them together, and then converting again to millig per liter as Ca3 so that they match the units of the rest of the values in the problem. And then finally using the bypass hardness equation to calculate the percent that should be bypassed. And that's it.

problem_statement: A 5 MGD water supply is treated with chlorine. The chlorine demand is 40% of the chlorine dose. If the free available chlorine concentration is measured to be 1.38 mg per liter, what was the chlorine dose supplied to the water in millig per liter? So, this is a super quick problem, but it's critical to understand exactly what chlorine demand is. And unfortunately, I don't see anything in either the civil or environmental reference manual to help with this. Let me know in the comments if you see something that could help a person with no background on this subject to get started. Thankfully, it's not hard. Chlorine demand is the amount of chlorine needed to react with substances in the water. The chlorine dose is simply the amount of chlorine supplied to the water. Therefore, the free available chlorine is the amount left over after subtracting the demand from the dose. So, the volume of the water supply is not going to be needed for this problem. So, let's just get rid of that. Now, we can see here that the chlorine demand is given as 40% of the dose. So we can say that we have the dose minus 40% of the dose.  And the free available chlorine is measured to be 1.38 mg per liter. So simplifying this down, the free available chlorine of 1.38 mg per liter is going to be equal to 100% of the dose minus 40% of the dose or 60% of the dose. If we divide both sides by 60 or rather 60%. Then we can see that the total dose is going to be 2 3 mg per liter which is our third option over here. So again, this problem is super easy. Just make sure to keep this concept in your head about the free available chlorine equaling the dose minus the demand. Or otherwise, find something in the reference manual that you can use to help jog your memory. And that's it.

topic: Landfill Gas Heating Value In  Pipeline (Dangit Bobby)
problem_statement: According to literature, landfill gas that is comprised of about 50% methane as CH4 and 50% carbon dioxide CO2 has a heating value of 500 BTUs per SCF. Some of this gas is used in a commercial pipeline which has a required heating value of 1,000 BTUs per SCF. If 9% of the gas in the pipeline is propane with a heating value of 2500 BTU per SCF, what is the actual percentage of methane in the landfill gas being used? So, this is a problem that we might see on the environmental exam. I'm not sure if there is anything in the reference manual that will be helpful here, but if you read the problem once or twice, you may realize that this is just a simple mass balance problem. Let's set up the mass balance by taking some key information from the problem statement. We can see that the total heating value in the pipeline needs to reach 1,000 BTUs per SCF. We are told that 9% of the gas in the pipeline is propane with a heating value of 2500 BTU per SCF. This means that we can figure out how much of the gas is also methane and from there determine its heating value. After we find its actual heating value, we can figure out what the actual percent of landfill gas is methane by comparing to the literature values provided. So 100% of the gas is in the pipeline minus the 9% propane means that 91% remains as methane. This will be our mass balance statement. So we can write 91% methane plus 9% propane*  2500 BTUs over SCF. Also note that SCF means standard cubic feet equals 100% of the 1,00 BTUs per. So solving for methane here we can see that the heating value of the methane in the pipe is about 851 BTUs per SCF.  Next, given that we know the heating value in the pipe and the heating value of 50% methane gas, we can determine the actual percent of methane in this specific landfills gas.  So setting up the ratio we can say that 50% overx is the same as 500 BTUs per SCF over 851 BTUs per SCF.  Writing this out a little bit more linearly, we can more easily solve for X, which we can see is going to come out to about 85%.  So this problem is very easy to solve as long as you understand the problem statement. Once you figure out the heating value of the methane mixed with propane in the pipeline, you can figure out the percentage of methane that the landfill gas is comprised of. And that's it.

topic: Incinerator Energy Balance with Missing Fractions
problem_statement: A town's mass burn incinerator has a name plate capacity of 500 tons per day. A new program begins to recycle newspaper, corrugated board, glass, aluminum, and ferrris cans with an overall efficiency of 50%. The waste stream composition and heating values are given in the table. On a particular day, the measured loss to the incinerator, otherwise known as the daily heat input removed due to recycling, is 500 million BTU per day. What percentage of the incoming waste stream is corrugated board? So in this problem, we are given a few things to start with, none of which has to come from a reference manual. We know the capacity of the incinerator is 500 tons per day and that half of this capacity is now being recycled for a specific set of items in the table. We also know the total heat loss to the incinerator aka the total amount of items being recycled expressed in BTU per day. Given this information, we are being asked to find the percent of corrugated board that is present in the waist stream. Since there are two unknowns in the waist stream, we can't simply sum them all and subtract from 100%. But since one of those unknowns, aluminum, has no BTU value, we can calculate and sum each item and then backsolve for what is missing from the total. So, let's mark down which items the problem is stating are included in recycling and calculate their BTU per day. We've got newspaper. Eventually, we're going to need to solve for corrugated board. There is ferris cans, aluminum, and glass. So, starting with newspaper, we can calculate the BTU per day as follows. The percentage of the waist stream times its specific heating value times the recycling efficiency time the capacity time the unit conversion of pounds per ton to get us to the proper units for newspaper. This brings us to 360 million BTUs per day. Skipping corrugated board for now, we can move on to ferris cans. I will write down the new value specific to that specific line item, but reference the constants in order to save time. So for ferris cans, it's 2.9% of the waist stream and 300 BTUs per pound. If we calculate this out with the other values in the equation, this gets us to 4,350,000 BTUs per day. For aluminum, we don't need to calculate anything since the heating value is zero. And for glass, we have 5% of the waist stream times 60 BTU per day times all of the other values referenced above. And this will get us to 1.5 million BTU per day. Summing these up, we can see that all line items recycled minus corrugated board comes to 365,850,000 BTU per day. So now we are ready to solve for our unknown percentage of corrugated board present in the waist stream. Let's write it out. So, our unknown percent in the waist stream times 7,000 BTUs per pound* 50% recycling time 500 tons per day time 2,000 lb per ton. And that's going to be equal to 500 millionUS 365,850,000. otherwise calculated to 134,150,000 BTU per day.  So simplifying the above equation we can see that we have 3.5 billion BTU per day * X equals 134,150,000 BTU per day. Solving for X, we can find that corrugated board is equal to about 3.8% of the total waist stream, which most closely resembles the second answer on the list. And that's it.

problem_statement: During a hazardous waste test burn, three designated principal organic hazardous constituents or PHC's are incinerated at 1,000° C. The waste feed stream was measured accurately, but the outlet concentration gauge malfunctioned. Fortunately, the monitoring computer still reports the destruction and removal efficiencies or DRE. Assuming the required DR is 99.99%, determine the present outlet concentration of the constituent in kilogram/ hour that is currently not in compliance. So this question is very easy to solve and is basically just here to get you familiar with another section in the reference manual. So we can see our given table down here requires each of our principal organic hazardous constituents and we have the inlet concentration that's going into the test burn for each one. We're missing the outlet concentration because the gauge is broken, but the monitoring computer is still giving us the actual um destruction and removal efficiencies. So, the question's asking us to pick the one that's not in compliance to find the outlet information for. So if we have 99.99% as our required DR, well the only one down here that doesn't meet that is tricloroethylene. So searching the reference manual for either DR or destruction and removal efficiency will take us straight to chapter 2 on air to a section called incineration on page 80. And this equation is just written as follows. So d r e equ= w in minus w out over w out time 100%. where DR is the destruction and removal efficiency, WIN is the mass feed rate of a particular principal organic hazardous constituent and W out is the mass emission rate of that same principal organic hazardous constituent. So, we're given all of the information we need to solve this problem right away. So, let's get to it. We can see that  our given DR for tricloroethylene is going to be 9975%. And that's going to be equal to our inlet concentration of 300. This is going to be kilograms per hour, but I'm just going to leave that off. minus our unknown W out which we want to find over the inlet again times 100%. So to simplify this equation we can drop the percentages from first each side of the equation and then divide by 100. So this will give us 0.99975 equals 300 - W out over 300 which if we rearrange the equations or if we simplify a little bit more we can multiply by 300 100 on each side to get 29925 equals 300 minus W out. And now if we rearrange we can see that W out equals 300 minus 29925 or 0.075 which is our third answer over here. And that's all it takes to solve this problem. The whole point of this particular question is just to get you familiar with the idea of test burns, principal organic hazardous constituents, and where to find the destruction and removal efficiency equation in the reference manual. And that's it. .

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #107: Environmental | Combustion Efficiency (7% O₂ Normalization)
problem_statement: A veterary clinic burns contaminated bedding and disposable supplies in its on-site incinerator. Stack tests of the incinerator gas show a measured CO concentration of 250 parts per million at 10% O2 on a dry basis. A measured CO2 concentration of 8,000 parts per million at 7% O2 on a dry basis. The EPA requires combustion efficiency reporting at concentrations of 7% O2 on a dry basis. The combustion efficiency is most nearly 94.5%, 96%, 97% or 99.9%. So the question is asking us for the combustion efficiency. If we search for this in the reference manual, it will take us to the following equation in chapter 2 on air where C combustion efficiency is equal to CO2 over CO2 plus CO * 100%. Where the volumes are in parts per million. So now how do we get the values we need for both CO2 and CO? Well, we can see that CO2 is already given at 7% O2 in the problem statement. So we can use that term directly. So, we're going to write here 8,000 parts per million over 8,000 parts per million plus CO. So, what about CO? There is another equation we can use from the reference manual as well. If we search for gas stream or 7% in the reference manual, this will bring us to the next equation just a little bit below the first equation. It's titled correcting particle concentrations in gas streams for 12% CO2 and 7% O2. Knowing to look for this equation might not be obvious at first. You would have to recognize that 7% O2 or 12% CO2 are common reference conditions used in combustion and air emission problems or that these are referred to as gas streams in regulatory language. If you didn't know that before studying, well, neither did I. And that's exactly why we study. So, let's look at the equation as it's written here. It provides spaces for both CO2 and O2. Now since our problem is only asking about O2, we can eliminate part of the equation related to CO2 correction. The measured CO2 is already at 7% O2. And because the percent of CO2 is not given for either CO or CO2, we have to use the O2 in this calculation. So to fill in this equation, we can substitute the term CP comma D with the 250 parts per million. Since this is the existing mass of the particullet per unit volume of dry gas for CO and in the problem statement we can see that measurement was made at 10% O2 but the EPA requires results reported at 7% O2. Then we can subtract 10 from 21 due to the percentage of oxygen in the CO. This is how we will normalize this term to the required 7% oxygen reporting requirement. So we'll have 14 on the top here and 21 - 10 for the 10% up here in the CO. Solving this out, we will get just about 318 parts per million. This is how we will normalize this term to the required 7% oxygen reporting requirement. Once this is done, we can go back to our combustion efficiency equation and plug in our terms for both CO2 which was given already at the correct percent of O2 and the CO which we just calculated. And that's it.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #119 Environmental | Radiation Intensity - Inverse Square Law
problem_statement: A radiation monitor is placed along a straight line between two sealed steel drums containing radioactive waste. Each drum has a diameter of 2 ft. Drum A produces a radiation intensity of 80 mR per hour at its surface and is located 4 ft center to monitor from the monitor. Drum B produces a radiation intensity of 180 mR per hour at its surface and is located on the opposite side of the monitor at an unknown distance center to monitor. If the total radiation measured at the monitor is 10 mR per hour, what is the distance in feet from the centers of drum A and drum B? Okay, so first let's sketch this problem out in case you are having difficulty understanding the problem statement. Here we have our extremely advanced radiation sensor. Over to the left will be drum A. Over to the right will be drum B. The statement notes that drum A produces a radiation intensity of 80 mR per hour and is located 4 ft away from the sensor from the center of the barrel. And we've been told as well that the drums have a diameter of 2 ft, so a radius of 1 ft. The radiation at drum B is 180 mR per hour, but we don't know the distance away from the monitor. Finally, we are given the radiation measurement at the monitor as 10 mR per hour. And we are being asked to find the total distance between the centers of both drums. So, if we first search for the word radiation in the reference manual, we will eventually get to a section about the inverse square law. It is written as follows. Intensity 1 over intensity 2 equals the square of radius 2 over the square of radius 1. So, this is the only equation we need to solve this problem. Let's do it in steps. First, we will find just the radiation contribution from drum A. So, intensity 1 is going to be the drum and that's 80 mR an hour. And intensity 2 is going to be unknown because we just want to find specifically drum A's contribution. The radius of 2 is 4 ft and the radius of the drum is going to be 1 ft. So, solving this out, we can see that we get 80 over 16 or 5 mR per hour. Now, we can subtract that from the total measured at the sensor to find drum B's radiation contribution as well. So, 10 minus 5 is going to be 5 mR per hour coming from drum B. Setting up the inverse square law equation again, we can say that intensity 1 this time will be the radiation from drum B and intensity 2 will be the radiation measured at the sensor. The radius 2 is going to be the radius from the sensor to the drum, which is unknown. And radius 1 is again going to be the radius of the drum. So, if we solve this out, we can see that our total distance between the sensor and the drum is going to be 6 ft. That means that step three, all we have to do is sum the distance from drum A to the sensor and drum B to the sensor or 4 + 6 to give us a final answer of 10 ft. So, this is one of those problems where understanding the concept is really important because you need to recognize that you need to solve for drum A's contribution first even though the total radiation at the sensor is already given. If you can figure that step out, obviously the math here is super easy and there's only three steps. And that's it.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #121 Environmental | EPA Hazard Index (Non-Cancer Risk) - Long Day Factory
topic: EPA Hazard Index (Non-Cancer Risk) - Long Day Factory
problem_statement: An unlucky individual is exposed to a chemical at the Long Day Factory at an intake rate of 0.00305 mg over kg days. Based on the EPA hazard index criteria, determine the minimum oral reference dose in mg over kg days required such that the adverse non-cancer health effects are not expected. So, this problem is actually very quick and easy to solve. In fact, the numerical value of the answer is technically already given to you. The only requirement is that you understand what the EPA hazard index actually is. This can be searched for in the reference manual. On page 143, the reference manual says directly that a hazard index greater than one represents the possibility of an adverse effect occurring. The manual also provides the following equation. Hazard index equals chronic daily intake in the context of non-carcinogenic health effects over the reference dose. Chronic daily intake itself is not specific to carcinogens or non-carcinogens. It is simply an exposure metric. When used with the reference dose in the hazard index equation, it is specifically evaluating non-cancer health risks. These could be things like damage to organs, neurological effects, or blood disorders. In reality, this means that our reference dose has to be any number equal to or greater than the chronic daily intake rate in order to keep the hazard index less than or equal to one. And since we are asked to find the minimum dose that will not trigger concern, we need to pick the value that keeps our ratio exactly equal to one. We can solve this out to be our second answer, or we can simply use the value of the intake rate if you understand the concept already. You may also notice the high level of precision among the multiple-choice answers here, which might feel frustrating. The level of precision in the answers would be annoying if this was a real calculation problem, but the minor differences between them are all actually intentional here to make sure that you understand the concept. If we selected 0.00304, this value is slightly lower than the intake rate, which would make the hazard index greater than one, indicating the potential for adverse effects, and therefore not meeting the acceptable threshold. Similarly, if we used 0.00306, this value is slightly higher than the intake rate, which would make the hazard index less than one, meaning it is acceptable, but not the minimum value that satisfies the threshold condition. So, understanding where to find hazard index and what it is are all that it takes to solve this problem. If you want to learn more about the hazard index, I will place a link to the EPA in the caption of the video description below.

problem_statement: During a break in the PE Exam, an engineer unwraps a Nature Valley granola bar. Upon the first bite, the bar behaves as expected and explodes into thousands of crumbs that scatter across the testing center. The mass of crumbs is determined to be log-normally distributed with a geometric standard deviation sigma g of 3 mm and a geometric mean crumb diameter of 5 mm. Approximately 86.4% of the crumbs are expected to have diameters less than what size in millimeters? So, this is a short problem statement that can potentially lead down a long rabbit hole if you're like me and bad at statistics. Let's walk through it in a simple way, describing only what you need to know. The problem statement mentions that the particle mass is log-normally distributed. Searching the reference manual for normal distribution returns one section that we can use. Page 172 provides a normal distribution function being given as z equals x minus mu over sigma. Being log-normally distributed means that the logarithm of the particle size is normally distributed. Therefore, when applying the z-score equation, we can replace x with natural log of x. Now, let's define our other terms. In the context of a normal distribution, the letter z represents a standardized score or a z-score. It measures exactly how many standard deviations a specific data point is away from the distribution's mean. A z-score is a statistical measurement that tells you how far away from the mean or average your data lies in a normally distributed sample. Mu is the mean of the normally distributed values. Since this problem is log-normally distributed and gives us the geometric mean, we can convert between the two using mu equals ln of X sub G. I also forgot to note before that the term X is the observed value, or in our case, the crumb particles. Sigma is the standard deviation of the logarithmically transformed values. Since the problem gives us a geometric standard deviation, we can convert using sigma equals natural log of sigma G. Now that we've made this distinction about some of our terms, we can fill them all in the equation. Z will need to be pulled from the normal distribution table a few pages away. In this table, the standardized variable is labeled X instead of Z. Since this is a standard normal distribution with a mean of zero and a standard deviation of one, the table's X values are equivalent to Z-scores. We have to know that Z is actually the column here labeled X and that we are looking for the values to the left of the curve, which is the column labeled capital F of X. Looking the capital F of X column for 0.864, we find a corresponding X value of approximately 1.1. In a standard normal table, this X value is equivalent to the Z score. So, as we go back to filling in this equation, we will leave X blank for now. Our geometric mean, X sub G, is going to be 5 as is given in the problem statement. And our sigma G value, originally sigma, from the original equation, is going to be 3. Next, we can rearrange the equation and then simplify by applying a given logarithmic property given in chapter 7. We can then apply one of the other logarithmic properties and rearrange the equation so that we are finally left with X equals 5 * 3 raised to the 1.1. Otherwise, calculate it out to 16.74. Leading our closest answer at the top here to be our final one of 17. So, the big takeaway here is not necessarily the final answer. And that's it.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #125 Water Resources/Environmental | LOAEL - Reference Dose of Burnout
problem_statement: A group of engineering students was monitored while preparing for the PE Exam. Researchers determined that the lowest observed adverse effect level, or LOAEL, for a substance known as caffeinium was 780 mg per day for an adult male engineer. At doses above this level, subjects began exhibiting symptoms of sadness, burnout, and repeatedly asking whether they should have gone into finance instead. An uncertainty factor of 10 and a modifying factor of 10 were applied to develop a reference dose. What is most nearly the resulting reference dose in milligrams over kilogram days? So, this problem is quick and easy to solve. The problem statement already tells you directly that it wants you to find the reference dose. For the environmental exam, you can search reference dose, and it will lead you directly to the following equation. RFD equals LOAEL over the uncertainty factor times the modifying factor. For the water resources exam, you can also search reference dose, or RFD, but it will lead you to a slightly different equation, and I'm not sure why. More about this in a minute. So, this equation is pretty simple. So, let's plug in our knowns. First, the LOAEL. The units are not specified in the environmental handbook, but they are for NOAEL as mg over kg * day. For some reason, in the water resources manual, the reference dose units are given instead. And that is also the units which the problem statement is asking for. So, the problem statement states that our LOAEL is 780 mg per day for an adult male engineer. Those last two words are important. They tell us that we need to include the body weight of an adult male in this problem in order to satisfy the required units. For the environmental homies, the reference manual provides an adult male body weight of 78 kg. For the WRE folks, this would need to be supplied as I don't think it's available in the water resources manual. So, our LOAEL will actually be 780 mg per day divided by 78 kg. And our uncertainty factor is given directly as 10, and our modifying factor is also given as 10. One final callout for the water resources exam. The reference manual equation only shows an uncertainty factor and does not explicitly include a modifying factor. If you encountered a problem like this on the exam, I would expect the wording to be clearer or for the modifying factor to be incorporated into an overall uncertainty factor. So, simplifying to the correct units, we can see that we get 10 mg over kg * days. Then, we can divide by 100 to get a final answer of 0.1 mg over kg days. This is identical to our first answer option at the top. So again, this problem is quick to solve as long as you pay attention to the units and don't forget to include body weight. If you do, there could be false answers that you might accidentally solve for on the exam. And that's it.

title: PE Exam Practice Problem #127 | Engineering Economics - Cost-Benefit Analysis
problem_statement: A warehouse measures 250 ft by 800 ft with a storage height of 24 ft. Due to the aisle requirements, 18% of the storage volume cannot be used for inventory. An automated storage system is proposed that reduces aisle space to nearly zero. The automated system costs $650,000 while the conventional shelving system costs $275,000. If the warehouse earns $18 per cubic yard of additional storage capacity, what is the net financial benefit of installing the automated system? So, this problem is a cost-benefit engineering economics problem and is really easy to solve. So, let's get into it. First, let's just get the warehouse volume in cubic feet. So, that's going to be 250 ft times 800 ft times 24 ft. And this will give us 4,000,000 800,000 cubic feet. Next, let's convert that to cubic yards since this is what the problem is going to ask for later. So, 4,000,000 800,000 cubic times 1 cubic yard over 3 feet cubed per cubic yard. That's basically 1 over 27 if you want to do a shortcut. And this will give us 177,000 777 cubic yards. Next, let's multiply by the 18% of storage volume that we could be getting back if we use an automated storage system. So, that's going to be 177,777 cubic yards times 0.18 which will give us 32,000 cubic yards. Now, we can find the value of those at $18 per cubic yard. So, 32,000 cubic yards times $18 per cubic yard equals $576,000. thousand dollars. So, now all we have to do is subtract the difference of the two system costs and compare it to the value of the space that we have recovered using the automated system. So, that will be 576 thousand dollars minus the difference of 650 minus 275 thousand dollars or the difference of 375. And that will give us 201 thousand dollars which is closest to our first answer over here. So, this is a really quick and easy problem to solve as long as you're paying attention to your units and recognizing that you need to account for the difference in costs of the two proposed systems. So, again we'll just compute the total volume, convert to cubic yards, multiply by the lost volume percentage, multiply by the value per cubic yard, and then subtract the additional cost of the automated system. And that's it.
